title: Inside the atom: the nuclear model
html:
Guiding question

How do the nuclei of atoms differ?

The answer to this question came from over 100 years of research, and how we know is often as interesting as what is known. In the late 1800s the atomic theory (matter is made of indivisible atoms that are rearranged in chemical reactions) was gaining popularity. The discovery of electricity and radioactivity then allowed scientists to study the structure of the atom itself.

UnderstandingStatement
Structure 1.2.1Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
Structure 1.2.2Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
Structure 1.2.3 (AHL)Mass spectra are used to determine the relative atomic masses of elements from their isotopic composition.

Atoms and the periodic table

Atoms are the smallest part of an element, and everything is made from them. The periodic table is not a random list: elements are arranged in order of atomic number, and the columns (groups) collect elements with similar chemistry. Why? Because chemistry is decided by electrons. Atoms react to reach a more stable arrangement of electrons, so the number of electrons in the outer energy level dictates how an atom reacts, and atoms with the same number of outer electrons show similar reactivity patterns.

GroupFamily nameMembers
1alkali metalsLi, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr
2alkaline earth metalsBe, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra
3 to 12transition elements (d-block)Sc to Zn in period 4, and below
17halogensF, Cl, Br, I, At
18noble gasesHe, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn

In the data booklet the element names are listed separately from the periodic table itself, with their symbols and atomic numbers, so quick recognition of symbols (Ge, K, V, Sb, Sc, Y...) saves real time in an exam.

The structure of the atom (Structure 1.2.1)

An atom contains a positively charged nucleus made of protons and neutrons (together called nucleons). Electrons occupy the vast region outside the nucleus. Protons, neutrons and electrons are the subatomic particles.

Key features of the nucleus:

  1. It is very small compared with the atom itself.
  2. It is highly dense and contains virtually all the mass of the atom.
  3. It has a positive charge.

Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1911)

How can we tell what is inside an atom if we cannot see it? Rutherford's answer was to fire something at it and watch what bounced off. Positively charged radioactive alpha particles were fired at a thin sheet of gold foil in a vacuum, and a movable detector around the foil recorded where they went: most passed through undeflected, some were deflected slightly, and a few were deflected through large angles.

ObservationRutherford's explanation
Most alpha particles pass straight through undeflectedThey pass through the empty space far from any nucleus: the nucleus is very small compared with the atom
Some alpha particles are deflected slightlyThey pass close to the positive nucleus and are repelled (like charges repel)
A few alpha particles bounce back off the nucleusThey hit the nucleus head-on; the nucleus is very dense and contains almost all the mass
Nature of science · FalsificationThe gold foil experiment falsified the model that preceded it, the "plum-pudding model", in which the atom was an amorphous positively charged blob with electrons spread throughout. If that were true, all alpha particles would have gone straight through the gold atoms undeflected. Rutherford's results contradicted the existing model and led to a new model of the atom. Scientific claims are falsifiable: they are vulnerable to evidence that contradicts them. A claim that survives severe testing is strong but can never be proven true with absolute certainty, so scientific knowledge always carries some uncertainty. Its provisional nature means further evidence can steer it in new directions. Question to consider: can a single counterexample falsify a claim?
Activity · Match observation to propertyMatch each gold foil observation with the property of the nucleus that explains it.
Nearly all alpha particles went straight through → the nucleus is very small compared with the size of the atom.
Occasionally some alpha particles bounced straight back → the nucleus is very dense, containing virtually all the mass of the atom.
Alpha particles are repelled when closely approaching the nucleus → the nucleus has a positive charge.

Which observation in the gold foil experiment shows that the nucleus is very small compared with the atom?

  1. A few alpha particles bounced back
  2. Most alpha particles passed straight through
  3. Some alpha particles were deflected slightly
  4. The foil became positively charged

If most particles meet nothing, the atom must be mostly empty space with a tiny nucleus. Bouncing back shows the nucleus is dense and massive; slight deflection shows it is positive.

The Rutherford (planetary) model

In 1911 Rutherford proposed the planetary model of the atom, also called the Rutherford model: a small central nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons on orbits around it. Negatively charged electrons orbit the positive nucleus as planets orbit the Sun. The Sun holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass; the nucleus holds over 99.9% of the atom's mass. The electrons are held in place by electrostatic attraction, not gravity.

Nature of science · ModelsScientists use models to represent natural phenomena; all models have limitations that should be identified and understood. In diagrams like these the size of the nucleus is greatly exaggerated, but they are still useful models. Scale analogy (Eden Park stadium, Auckland): if the atom were the size of a stadium, the nucleus would be a golf ball at the centre of the pitch, and you in the top row of seats would be an electron. The diameter of an atom is about 100 000 times the diameter of the nucleus, so the nucleus occupies a tiny volume of the atom.
Most atoms have diameters of 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ to 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Units for atomic dimensions:
picometre: 1 pm = 10⁻¹² m
angstrom (used in X-ray crystallography): 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m
Conversions use dimensional analysis (multiply by conversion factors so units cancel). Rutherford's work, despite its limitations, is the basis of our thinking about atomic structure. He is rumoured to have said: "All science is either physics or stamp collecting!"
Worked example · pm to ÅThe atomic radius of fluorine is 60 × 10⁻¹² m (60 pm). Convert to Å.
60 pm × (10⁻¹² m / 1 pm) × (1 Å / 10⁻¹⁰ m)
= 0.60 Å = 6.0 × 10⁻¹ Å

A carbon atom has a diameter of 150 pm. Convert this to ångströms.

150 pm × (10⁻¹² m / 1 pm) × (1 Å / 10⁻¹⁰ m) = 1.5 Å. Shortcut: 1 Å = 100 pm, so divide pm by 100.
TOKThe models discussed assume atoms are real, but it could be argued objects are only "real" when they can be seen. In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer (IBM, Zurich) invented the scanning tunnelling microscope (STM), which produces three-dimensional images of surfaces at the atomic level, allowing individual atoms to be observed directly. They won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics. IBM made an atomic-scale film, A Boy and his Atom, by moving individual atoms to draw a stick figure. Questions: Has technology extended humans' capacity to make observations of the natural world? How important are material tools in the production or acquisition of knowledge?

Subatomic particles

Later experiments showed the nucleus also contains a neutral particle, the neutron, with nearly the same mass as the proton.

ParticleRelative massRelative chargeLocation
proton1+1nucleus
neutron10nucleus
electronnegligible (≈ 1/1836, about 5 × 10⁻⁴)−1outside nucleus (shells / energy levels)

The charge on one electron is the elementary charge, e ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Charges of subatomic particles are usually given in elementary charge units: electron −e, proton +e. The symbol e is often omitted, so electrons and protons are said to have charges of −1 and +1. The actual masses and charges are in the data booklet (section 4): proton 1.672622 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, neutron 1.674927 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, electron 9.109383 × 10⁻³¹ kg; charges +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C for the proton, 0 for the neutron and −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C for the electron (note the minus sign).

  3. List the values in order of increasing size. Was your first list correct?

  5. (ATL) Give the full reference for your sources using your school's referencing system.

Increasing order: proton < carbon atom < I–I bond < C₆₀ < paper < onion cell < full stop.

Which statement about the electron is correct?

  1. It has a relative mass of 1 and a charge of −1
  2. It is found in the nucleus
  3. It has the same mass as a proton but the opposite charge
  4. Its mass is about 1/1836 of a proton's and its charge is −1

The electron's charge is equal and opposite to the proton's, but its mass is tiny, so it is treated as negligible when we add up the mass of an atom.

title: Atomic number, mass number and ions
html:
Atomic number and mass number

As of 2023 there are 118 known elements, with atomic numbers 1 to 118.

  • Atomic number (Z) = number of protons in the nucleus. It identifies the element and never changes when an ion forms. Gold (Z = 79) has 79 protons; carbon (Z = 6) has 6.
  • Mass number (A) = number of protons + neutrons. Since all the relative mass is in the nucleus, number of neutrons N = A − Z. Gold: A = 197, so 197 − 79 = 118 neutrons.
  • A neutral atom has no overall charge, so number of electrons = number of protons.
A = Z + NN = A − Z

Nuclear symbol notation AZX (mass number A top left, atomic number Z bottom left, chemical symbol X) shows the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons. Gold: ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au. Sodium: ²³₁₁Na has 11 protons, 11 electrons and 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons. For ⁷₃Li: 3 protons, so it must have 3 electrons, and 7 − 3 = 4 neutrons.

Common mistakeThe top number in a nuclear symbol is the mass number (a whole number for one particular atom), not the relative atomic mass. Lithium's Ar on the periodic table is 6.94, an average over its isotopes; the "7" in ⁷₃Li counts the protons and neutrons in one atom of lithium-7.
Work out all six, then reveal

Hydrogen-1 is the only atom with no neutrons at all.

Where the mass number was not given (e.g. barium, calcium), use the mass number of the most common isotope; the "sodium-24" row is a radioactive isotope of sodium (the stable one is sodium-23).

Ions

Atoms form compounds by sharing or transferring electrons, so they may end up with more or fewer electrons than protons. Such a charged particle is an ion. Charge of ion = number of protons − number of electrons.

  • Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form the ionic compound magnesium oxide. Mg loses two electrons: 12 protons, 10 electrons, so a 2+ charge: ²⁴₁₂Mg²⁺ (mass number 24 = 12 protons + 12 neutrons; charge written top right).
  • Oxygen gains the two electrons lost by magnesium to form the oxide ion, ¹⁶₈O²⁻.
Mg + ½O₂ → Mg²⁺ + O²⁻

This chemical equation is more commonly written with the product as MgO. The opposite charges on Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ attract each other; this attraction is an ionic bond. Ionic bonds hold the ions together in solid magnesium oxide (ionic bonding is covered further in Structure 2.1).

Counting particles: a reliable routine

  1. Protons = atomic number Z, which identifies the element. It never changes when an ion forms.
  2. Neutrons = A − Z (mass number minus atomic number).
  3. Electrons = Z − charge. A 2+ ion has lost 2 electrons; a 3− ion has gained 3.
Worked examples²⁴Mg²⁺: 12 protons, 24 − 12 = 12 neutrons, 12 − 2 = 10 electrons.
An atom X with A = 63 and 34 neutrons: Z = 63 − 34 = 29, so X is copper (29 electrons if neutral).
A species with 31 protons, 40 neutrons and 28 electrons: Ga (Z = 31), A = 71, charge = 31 − 28 = 3+ → ⁷¹Ga³⁺.
Activity · Nuclear symbol of an ionDeduce the nuclear symbol for an ion with 24 protons, 21 electrons and 28 neutrons. Answer: Z = 24 (chromium), A = 24 + 28 = 52, charge = 24 − 21 = +3, so ⁵²₂₄Cr³⁺.

How many electrons are in a ³²₁₆S²⁻ ion?

Electrons = Z − charge = 16 − (−2) = 18. (It also has 16 protons and 32 − 16 = 16 neutrons.)

Which statement is always correct for any atom or ion?

  1. Number of protons = number of electrons
  2. Number of protons = number of neutrons
  3. Number of protons = atomic number
  4. Mass number = number of neutrons

Protons = electrons only for a neutral atom. Neutrons = protons only for some light isotopes (¹²C, ¹⁶O), not in general. The atomic number is defined as the number of protons, so that one is always true.

Identify the particle (class challenge): predict each, then reveal
  1. An atom with 6 protons and the same number of neutrons as a ¹⁴N atom → 6 p, 7 n → ¹³C
  2. An atom with one more proton and the same number of neutrons as ³⁹K → 20 p, 20 n → ⁴⁰Ca
  3. An atom with 10 protons and the same number of neutrons as ²⁴Mg → 10 p, 12 n → ²²Ne
  4. An atom with one less proton and the same number of neutrons as ⁶⁶Zn → 29 p, 36 n → ⁶⁵Cu
  5. An atom with the same number of protons and two more neutrons than ⁷⁹Br → ⁸¹Br
  6. An atom with two fewer protons and the same number of neutrons as ⁵⁰Cr → 22 p, 26 n → ⁴⁸Ti
  7. An ion with one more proton and two more neutrons than ²⁰Ne but the same number of electrons → 11 p, 12 n, 10 e → ²³Na⁺
  8. An ion with two fewer protons and two fewer neutrons than ⁴⁰Ar but the same number of electrons → 16 p, 20 n, 18 e → ³⁶S²⁻
  9. An ion with two more protons and two more neutrons than ⁶⁰Ni but the same number of electrons → 30 p, 34 n, 28 e → ⁶⁴Zn²⁺
  10. An ion with two more protons and three more neutrons than ²⁰Ne but the same number of electrons → 12 p, 13 n, 10 e → ²⁵Mg²⁺
  11. An ion with one less proton, one less neutron and the same number of electrons as ¹²⁹Xe → 53 p, 74 n, 54 e → ¹²⁷I⁻
  12. An ion with one more proton, two more neutrons but the same number of electrons as ⁸⁵Rb⁺ → 38 p, 50 n, 36 e → ⁸⁸Sr²⁺
  13. A particle with two fewer protons, two fewer neutrons and the same number of electrons as ²⁰Ne → 8 p, 8 n, 10 e → ¹⁶O²⁻
  14. A particle with one less proton, two fewer neutrons and one more electron than ⁴⁸Ti²⁺ → 21 p, 24 n, 21 e → ⁴⁵Sc (a neutral atom)
  15. A particle with one less proton, two more neutrons and the same number of electrons as ¹²⁷I⁻ → 52 p, 76 n, 54 e → ¹²⁸Te²⁻
Exam tipExam-style "give the symbol" questions want both numbers: an atom with 12 neutrons and 11 electrons is ²³₁₁Na (Z = 11 because a neutral atom has as many protons as electrons; A = 11 + 12 = 23). When defining atomic number, say "the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom"; "protons and electrons" loses the mark.

title: Isotopes and relative atomic mass
html:
Isotopes (Structure 1.2.2)

Every type of atom has a characteristic mass. So why does the periodic table give chlorine a relative atomic mass of 35.45? You cannot have 0.45 of a proton.

The answer is isotopes: different atoms of the same element with a different number of neutrons. They have different mass numbers, A, but the same atomic number, Z. Think of the teacher's Ford Fiesta analogy: the same car model comes in several versions that differ in a few details but are all, unmistakably, Fiestas. Isotopes are different versions of one element.

  • Chlorine has two isotopes: ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl.
  • Isotopes have similar chemical properties (same number of electrons) but different physical properties, such as density, because atoms of one isotope are heavier than atoms of the other.
  • Naturally occurring hydrogen has two stable isotopes: hydrogen-1 (protium) and hydrogen-2 (deuterium). The third, hydrogen-3 (tritium), is radioactive and does not occur in nature in significant amounts.

A portable tritium light source works because tritium decays, emitting high-energy electrons (beta particles) that hit a fluorescent material and make it glow in the dark.

Activity · Hydrogen isotopes
IsotopeNuclear symbolZNA
hydrogen-1 (protium)¹₁H101
hydrogen-2 (deuterium)²₁H112
hydrogen-3 (tritium)³₁H123

The atomic number is often omitted from isotope symbols, e.g. ³⁷Cl: the symbol Cl already tells you Z = 17. Isotopes can also be written with a hyphen: chlorine-37 or Cl-37. The name comes from Greek iso-topos, "same place": isotopes occupy the same place in the periodic table.

Key definition: isotopes are different atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.

Physical properties of isotopes

Isotopes have the same nuclear charge and differ only in the number of neutrons. Neutrons do not affect electron configuration (Structure 1.3), so chemical properties are nearly identical. Physical properties differ noticeably (density, rate of diffusion, melting and boiling points), especially for compounds containing hydrogen isotopes, where the mass doubles.

CompoundDensity at 4 °C / g cm⁻³Melting point / °CBoiling point / °C
¹H₂O (normal water)1.0000.00100.0
²H₂O (heavy water, D₂O)1.1063.82101.4
  • Natural uranium consists mainly of ²³⁵U and ²³⁸U. Differences in their physical properties are used for enrichment: increasing the proportion of ²³⁵U over ²³⁸U in nuclear fuel (enriched uranium is made into small fuel pellets). Most reactors need at least 3% ²³⁵U; natural uranium has only 0.72%.
  • Enriching one isotope in a substance also lets chemists track reaction mechanisms and progress: isotope labelling.

Why do ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl have the same chemical properties?

  1. They have the same number of electrons, arranged in the same way
  2. They have the same mass number
  3. They have the same number of neutrons
  4. They have the same density

Chemistry is decided by electrons, and both isotopes have 17 electrons in the same arrangement. Mass number, neutrons and density all differ.

Isotope tracers

Isotopes can be used as markers to keep track of the positions of atoms during a chemical change. A reactant A can often turn into product B by more than one pathway. One atom in a reactant is replaced by a different isotope (e.g. ¹⁸O instead of ¹⁶O, or ²H instead of ¹H). The reaction is carried out as usual and the products are analysed by mass spectrometry to see where the labelled atom ends up. This shows which bonds broke and supports one reaction mechanism over another. A classic example: in esterification with ¹⁸O-labelled ethanol, the ¹⁸O appears in the ester, not the water, showing that the C–O bond in the alcohol is not broken (linking question with R3.4).

Relative atomic mass and natural abundance

  • The relative atomic mass, Ar, on the periodic table is not a whole number because it is the weighted average of all the isotopes of that element, taking into account both their masses and their relative abundances (amounts). It is measured relative to one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
  • Natural abundance (NA) of an isotope is the percentage of its atoms among all atoms of that element found on Earth.
  • If all natural abundances are known, the average Ar can be calculated. The reverse (abundances from Ar) is only possible if the element has two known isotopes.
  • Average Ar values for all elements are in the data booklet and periodic table.
Ar = Σ(A × NA)100
Exam tip · defining Ar (2 marks)Relative atomic mass = the weighted average mass of the atoms of an element (1) compared with 1/12 of the mass of one atom of carbon-12 (1). Writing "mass number" instead of "mass" scores zero.
Worked example 1 · Ar of ironIsotopes and natural abundances: ⁵⁴Fe 5.845%, ⁵⁶Fe 91.754%, ⁵⁷Fe 2.119%, ⁵⁸Fe 0.282%. Calculate Ar.
Abundances add up to 100%, so divide by 100
Ar = (54 × 5.845 + 56 × 91.754 + 57 × 2.119 + 58 × 0.282) / 100
= 5590.99 / 100 = 55.91
(The data booklet value is 55.85: using exact isotopic masses instead of whole mass numbers gives the more accurate answer.)
Worked example 2 · Abundances of chlorine isotopesChlorine has two stable isotopes, Cl-35 and Cl-37. Ar = 35.45. Calculate the natural abundance of each.
Ar = [(A₁ × NA₁) + (A₂ × NA₂)] / 100
Let x = NA of Cl-35, so 100 − x = NA of Cl-37
[35x + 37(100 − x)] / 100 = 35.45
(3700 − 2x) / 100 = 35.45
x = (3700 − 3545) / 2 = 77.5
Cl-35 = 77.5%, Cl-37 = 22.5%

The actual abundances of ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl are 75.8% and 24.2%. The calculated values differ because mass numbers were used; these are rounded values of the actual isotopic masses.

  • Sanity check: Ar must lie between the lightest and heaviest isotope masses, and closer to the more abundant one. For an element that is mostly ²⁴X with some ²⁵X and ²⁶X, the answer is "between 24 and 25".
  • Unknown abundance: let one abundance be x and the other (100 − x), then solve. Example: boron, Ar = 10.81, isotopes ¹⁰B and ¹¹B. 10x + 11(100 − x) = 1081 → x = 19%, so ¹⁰B is 19% and ¹¹B is 81%.
Worked example · oxygen¹⁶O 99.76%, ¹⁷O 0.04%, ¹⁸O 0.20%.
Ar = (16 × 99.76 + 17 × 0.04 + 18 × 0.20) ÷ 100 = 1600.44 ÷ 100 = 16.00 (2 d.p.)
Common mistakeReading the Ar from the periodic table as the mass number. A mass number is always a whole number for one specific isotope. Chlorine's 35.45 is an average, so you cannot calculate "18.45 neutrons".

Lithium: ⁶Li 7.59%, ⁷Li 92.41%. Calculate Ar to 2 d.p.

(6 × 7.59 + 7 × 92.41) ÷ 100 = (45.54 + 646.87) ÷ 100 = 6.92 (data booklet: 6.94).

Chromium: ⁵⁰Cr 4.35%, ⁵²Cr 83.79%, ⁵³Cr 9.50%, ⁵⁴Cr 2.36%. Calculate Ar to 2 d.p.

(50 × 4.35 + 52 × 83.79 + 53 × 9.50 + 54 × 2.36) ÷ 100 = (217.5 + 4357.08 + 503.5 + 127.44) ÷ 100 = 5205.52 ÷ 100 = 52.06 (data booklet: 52.00). The other rows: B 10.80, Mg 24.32, Si 28.11.

Rubidium has two common isotopes: ⁸⁵Rb (72.2%) and ⁸⁷Rb (27.8%). Calculate the average atomic mass.

(85 × 72.2 + 87 × 27.8) ÷ 100 = (6137 + 2418.6) ÷ 100 = 85.56.
More from the average-atomic-mass worksheet (with checked answers)
  1. Uranium: ²³⁴U 0.01%, ²³⁵U 0.71%, ²³⁸U 99.28% → Ar = 237.98.
  2. Titanium: ⁴⁶Ti 8.0%, ⁴⁷Ti 7.8%, ⁴⁸Ti 73.4%, ⁴⁹Ti 5.5%, ⁵⁰Ti 5.3% → 47.92.
  3. Chlorine in swimming pools: 75.53% ³⁵Cl (mass 34.969) and 24.47% ³⁷Cl (mass 36.966) → 35.46.
  4. Copper: ⁶³Cu has mass 62.9298 and abundance 69.09%; ⁶⁵Cu has abundance 30.91%; Ar = 63.546. Mass of ⁶⁵Cu = (63.546 × 100 − 62.9298 × 69.09) ÷ 30.91 = 64.923. (The real mass of ⁶⁵Cu is 64.928; the small gap comes from rounding in the data given.)
  5. Neon: Ne-20 (19.992, 90.51%), Ne-21 (20.994), Ne-22 (9.22%), average 20.179. Abundance of Ne-21 = 100 − 90.51 − 9.22 = 0.27%; mass of Ne-22 = (2017.9 − 19.992 × 90.51 − 20.994 × 0.27) ÷ 9.22 = 21.991.
  6. Why is carbon's Ar 12.011 when a carbon-12 atom has a mass of exactly 12? Because 12.011 is the weighted average of all carbon atoms, including about 1.1% of the heavier carbon-13 (and a trace of carbon-14). The carbon-12 atom itself is exactly 12 by definition.

A note on one worksheet question: a magnesium problem giving abundances of 78.70%, 10.13% and 11.7% cannot be solved reliably, because those percentages add up to 100.53%, not 100%. The real values are 78.99%, 10.00% and 11.01%, which give Ar = 24.305 as in the handwritten example above.

Practice questions
  1. State the nuclear symbols for potassium-39 and copper-65. Deduce the numbers of protons and neutrons in each nucleus. (³⁹₁₉K: 19 p, 20 n; ⁶⁵₂₉Cu: 29 p, 36 n.)
  2. Sulfur has four isotopes: ³²S (95.02%), ³³S (0.75%), ³⁴S (4.21%), ³⁶S (0.02%). Calculate the average Ar.
  3. The actual Ar of sulfur is 32.07. Suggest why your answer differs.

Practice question 2: calculate the Ar of sulfur to 2 d.p.

(32 × 95.02 + 33 × 0.75 + 34 × 4.21 + 36 × 0.02) ÷ 100 = (3040.64 + 24.75 + 143.14 + 0.72) ÷ 100 = 3209.25 ÷ 100 = 32.09. It differs from 32.07 because whole-number mass numbers were used instead of the exact isotopic masses (which are slightly less than the mass numbers for these isotopes).
Global impact of scienceScientific developments can have ethical, environmental, political, social, cultural and economic consequences. Nuclear fission (splitting large nuclei, releasing huge amounts of energy) led to nuclear energy and the atomic bomb. Element 109, meitnerium (Mt), is named after Lise Meitner, the second woman to receive a physics doctorate from the University of Vienna. Her work with Otto Frisch led to the discovery of nuclear fission, published in Nature in 1939. She declined to work on the US atomic bomb, saying "I will have nothing to do with a bomb!" Question: what other scientific developments have had important ethical implications?
Summary questions(1) What is an isotope, and what effect does the extra neutron have on the atom? (2) Explain how to calculate Ar, with an example. (3) Explain how isotopes can provide evidence for a reaction mechanism.
Linking question (AHL)How can isotope tracers provide evidence for a reaction mechanism? (Reactivity 3.4)

title: Mass spectrometry
html:
Mass spectrometry (Structure 1.2.3) AHL

Where do the isotopic abundances in the last lesson come from? They are measured with a mass spectrometer, an instrument that detects the relative abundance of isotopes in a sample by measuring the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of ions.

  1. Vaporization: the sample is injected and vaporized by a heating filament.
  2. Ionization: atoms are bombarded with a beam of high-energy electrons and lose electrons to form positive ions (cations), e.g. Cu(g) + e⁻ → Cu⁺(g) + 2e⁻. (Modern instruments may also use chemical ionisation, electrospray or a laser.)
  3. Acceleration: positive ions are accelerated by an electric field.
  4. Deflection (separation): ions are deflected by a magnetic field. The degree of deflection depends on the mass to charge ratio (m/z). Uncharged particles are not affected and never reach the detector. Lowest m and highest z are deflected most; the heaviest particles are deflected least. (Time-of-flight instruments instead separate ions by how long they take to reach the detector.)
  5. Detection: the m/z values of ions hitting the detector are passed to a computer, which produces the mass spectrum: relative abundance (intensity) of detected ions plotted against m/z.

The operational details of the mass spectrometer will not be assessed in examination papers, but this outline helps you read spectra.

  • Ions with a smaller m/z are deflected more. A 2+ ion has half the m/z of the 1+ ion of the same mass, so it is deflected more.
  • Uses: identifying unknown compounds from their molecular mass, measuring isotope abundances, gaining information about the structure of molecules, drug testing in sport, monitoring patients' breath during surgery, analysing molecules in space and detecting toxic chemicals in marine life.

Which ion is deflected most in a magnetic-sector mass spectrometer?

  1. ³⁷Cl⁺
  2. ³⁵Cl⁺
  3. ⁷⁰Cl₂⁺
  4. ³⁵Cl²⁺

Deflection depends on m/z: the smaller m/z, the greater the deflection. ³⁵Cl²⁺ has m/z = 35 ÷ 2 = 17.5, the smallest of the four.

Reading a mass spectrum AHL

Each peak corresponds to one isotope (for singly charged ions, m/z = mass number). Its height gives the relative abundance. Copper's spectrum, for example, shows two peaks: m/z 63 (relative intensity 100) and m/z 65 (about 45 on that scale, i.e. abundances of about 69% and 31%).

When the peaks are given as percentages, divide by 100. When they are given as relative intensities that do not add up to 100 (the tallest peak is often set to 100), divide by the sum of the intensities instead.

Worked example 3 · Ar of boron from a mass spectrumMass spectrum of boron with peaks at m/z 10 (relative intensity 19.9) and m/z 11 (80.1). Calculate Ar.
m/z 10 → isotope of mass number 10, abundance 19.9%
m/z 11 → isotope of mass number 11, abundance 80.1%
Abundances add up to 100, so divide by 100
Ar = (11 × 80.1 + 10 × 19.9) / 100 = 10.8

Use the spectrum of X to calculate its relative atomic mass to one decimal place.

The abundances add up to 3 + 4 + 1 + 5 = 13, so divide by 13, not 100:
Ar = (70 × 3 + 72 × 4 + 73 × 1 + 74 × 5) ÷ 13 = 941 ÷ 13 = 72.4. X is germanium (Ar 72.63 in the data booklet).
(a) Define relative atomic mass; (c) identify the ion responsible for the peak at m/z 72

(a) The weighted average mass of the atoms of an element (1), relative to 1/12 of the mass of one atom of carbon-12 (1). Any wording that compares the average atomic mass with carbon-12 taken as exactly 12 is acceptable; using "mass number" instead of "mass" scores zero.

(c) ⁷²Ge⁺. The charge must be shown: the detector only sees ions.

Data-based questions
  1. The mass spectrum of an unknown element has peaks at m/z 204 (about 0.2), 206 (about 2.4), 207 (about 2.2) and 208 (about 5.2). Estimate abundances, calculate Ar and identify the element. (Ar ≈ 207.2, lead.)
  2. Mass spectrometry detects specific elements in geological samples, including those of cosmic origin. Cobalt and nickel are common in iron meteorites (for example the Tamentit iron meteorite, found in 1864 in the Sahara). They have similar properties and nearly identical Ar, but very different isotopic compositions, so mass spectrometry distinguishes them easily. Nickel shows peaks at m/z 58 (100), 60 (about 38), 61 (about 2) and 62 (about 5); cobalt shows a single peak at m/z 59 (100). Estimate nickel's abundances, calculate its Ar and decide which metal has the larger Ar. (Ni ≈ 58.7, Co = 59, so cobalt is larger, even though nickel has the higher atomic number.)
  3. The actual Ar of nickel is 58.69. Suggest why your result differs. (Peak heights were estimated from a graph and whole-number masses were used.)

Nickel: peaks at m/z 58 (100), 60 (38), 61 (2) and 62 (5). Calculate Ar to 1 d.p.

Sum of intensities = 100 + 38 + 2 + 5 = 145.
Ar = (58 × 100 + 60 × 38 + 61 × 2 + 62 × 5) ÷ 145 = (5800 + 2280 + 122 + 310) ÷ 145 = 8512 ÷ 145 = 58.7.

Molecules in the mass spectrometer AHL

When a compound is analysed, gaseous molecules are bombarded with high-speed electrons. These knock an electron out of some of the molecules, creating molecular ions: M(g) + e⁻ → M⁺(g) + 2e⁻. For a compound, the peak with the highest m/z is usually the molecular ion, and its m/z equals Mr. Some molecular ions break apart into fragments, giving peaks at lower m/z; the fragmentation pattern is used for structure determination in S3.2.

Exam tip · diatomic elements A spectrum of chlorine gas shows peaks for atoms (m/z 35 and 37) and for Cl₂⁺ molecules at m/z 70 (³⁵Cl³⁵Cl), 72 (³⁵Cl³⁷Cl) and 74 (³⁷Cl³⁷Cl). With 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl, the molecular peaks are in the ratio 9 : 6 : 1. When you read an element's spectrum to find Ar, use only the single-atom peaks.
Why 9 : 6 : 1? Predict, then reveal

Pick two chlorine atoms at random. P(³⁵Cl³⁵Cl) = 0.75 × 0.75 = 0.5625. P(³⁷Cl³⁷Cl) = 0.25 × 0.25 = 0.0625. P(one of each) = 2 × 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.375 (the factor 2 because either atom can be the heavy one). 0.5625 : 0.375 : 0.0625 = 9 : 6 : 1.

In the mass spectrum of a pure compound, the peak at the highest m/z is at 46. What does this tell you?

  1. The compound's most abundant fragment has a mass of 46
  2. The relative molecular mass of the compound is about 46
  3. The compound contains an isotope of mass number 46
  4. The compound contains 46 atoms

The highest-m/z peak is (usually) the molecular ion M⁺, so Mr ≈ 46 (ethanol, C₂H₅OH, for example). The tallest peak, the base peak, is often a fragment instead.
